#### Proof of Theorem 3.7.

We shall now estimate the production term in Proposition 6.1 which depends on the temperature. Integrating by parts in $\mathrm{d}z$ and using the boundary condition gives

$$ \int\bm{u}\cdot\nabla\times\nabla\times T\bm{e}_{z}\,\mathrm{d}V=-\langle\partial_{z}\bm{u},\overline{\nabla\times\nabla\times T\bm{e}_{z}}\rangle, $$

where recall $\overline{\vphantom{i}\cdot\vphantom{i}}$ indicates the vertical primitive. The curl of the momentum equation (2.1a) is

$$ -\partial_{z}\bm{u}=\Lambda\nabla\times(\bm{J}\times\bm{B})+\mbox{{Ra}}\nabla\times T\bm{e_{z}}+\mbox{{Ek}}\nabla\times\nabla^{2}\bm{u}. $$

Observe that the middle term is toroidal, and therefore is orthogonal to the poloidal field $\overline{\nabla\times\nabla\times T\bm{e}_{z}}$ such that

$$ \langle\nabla\times T\bm{e_{z}},\overline{\nabla\times\nabla\times T\bm{e}_{z}}\rangle=-\langle\nabla\times\overline{T}\bm{e_{z}},\nabla\times\nabla\times T\bm{e}_{z}\rangle=0. $$

For the last term, we integrate by parts

$$ \displaystyle\langle\nabla\times\nabla^{2}\bm{u},\overline{\nabla\times\nabla\times T\bm{e}_{z}}\rangle+\int\bm{n}_{\pm}\cdot(\nabla^{2}\bm{u}\times\overline{\nabla\times\nabla\times T\bm{e}_{z}})\,\mathrm{d}S_{\pm} \displaystyle=\langle\nabla^{2}\bm{u},\nabla\times\overline{\nabla\times\nabla\times T\bm{e}_{z}}\rangle. $$

By the poloidal structure of $\overline{\nabla\times\nabla\times T\bm{e}_{z}}$ , the boundary term vanishes. Pointwise on $S_{\pm}$ it holds

$$ \displaystyle\bm{n}_{\pm}\cdot(\nabla^{2}\bm{u}\times\overline{\nabla\times\nabla\times T\bm{e}_{z}}) \displaystyle=-\nabla^{2}\bm{u}\cdot(\bm{n}_{\pm}\times\overline{\nabla\times\nabla\times T\bm{e}_{z}})=-\nabla^{2}\bm{u}\cdot(\overline{\nabla^{\perp}_{x,y}\partial_{z}T})=-\nabla^{2}\bm{u}\cdot\nabla^{\perp}_{x,y}T=0, $$

where the last equality holds by the isothermal boundary conditions. Therefore, we have established the identity

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mbox{{Ra}}}{\Lambda}\int\bm{u}\cdot\nabla\times\nabla\times T\bm{e}_{z}\,\mathrm{d}V \displaystyle=\mbox{{Ra}}\,\langle\nabla\times(\bm{J}\times\bm{B}),\overline{\nabla\times\nabla\times T\bm{e}_{z}}\rangle+\frac{\mbox{{Ra}}\,\mbox{{Ek}}}{\Lambda}\langle\nabla^{2}\bm{u},\nabla\times\overline{\nabla\times\nabla\times T\bm{e}_{z}}\rangle. $$

Because $\bm{B}$ and $\bm{J}$ are divergence free, it holds pointwise

$$ \nabla\times(\bm{J}\times\bm{B})=(\bm{B}\cdot\nabla)\bm{J}-(\bm{J}\cdot\nabla)\bm{B}. $$

By Hölder’s inequality, it then follows

$$ \displaystyle\langle\nabla\times(\bm{J}\times\bm{B}),\overline{\nabla\times\nabla\times T\bm{e}_{z}}\rangle\leq\|\overline{\nabla\times\nabla\times T\bm{e}_{z}}\|_{L^{2}}\left(\|\bm{B}\|_{L^{\infty}}\|\nabla\bm{J}\|_{L^{2}}+\|\bm{J}\|_{L^{6}}\|\nabla\bm{B}\|_{L^{3}}\right) $$

We now recall the Sobolev embeddings $H^{2}(V)\hookrightarrow L^{\infty}(V)$ , the Ladyzhenskaya and Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequalities. These estimates are,

$$ \|\bm{J}\|_{L^{6}}\leq C_{\mathrm{S}}\|\nabla\bm{J}\|_{L^{2}},\quad\|\bm{B}\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C_{b}(\|\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}}+\|\nabla\bm{J}\|_{L^{2}}),\quad\|\nabla\bm{B}\|_{L^{3}}^{2}\leq C_{\mathrm{S}}\|\nabla\bm{J}\|_{L^{2}}\|\bm{J}\|_{L^{2}}. $$

We used the fact that $\bm{B}$ is divergence free, and recalled that the ferromagnetic boundary conditions and exact magnetic flux identity ensure the kernel of the curl operator is trivial. With the embeddings (6.43) and the Poincaré inequality, this implies

$$ \langle\nabla\times(\bm{J}\times\bm{B}),\overline{\nabla\times\nabla\times T\bm{e}_{z}}\rangle\leq C_{n}\|\overline{\nabla\times\nabla\times T\bm{e}_{z}}\|_{L^{2}}\int|\nabla\bm{J}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}V, $$

where

$$ C_{n}=C_{b}(1+C_{\mathrm{P}}^{2}+C_{\mathrm{P}}^{4})^{1/2}+C^{3/2}_{\mathrm{S}}C_{\mathrm{P}}^{1/2}. $$

On the other hand, by Young’s inequality it holds

$$ \displaystyle\langle\nabla^{2}\bm{u},\nabla\times\overline{\nabla\times\nabla\times T\bm{e}_{z}}\rangle \displaystyle\leq\frac{\mbox{{Ra}}\,\Lambda\,}{\,\mbox{{Ek}}^{\gamma}}\|\nabla\times\overline{\nabla\times\nabla\times T\bm{e}_{z}}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\int|\nabla\bm{J}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}V+\frac{\mbox{{Ek}}^{\gamma}}{4\mbox{{Ra}}\Lambda\|\nabla\bm{J}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}\int|\nabla^{2}\bm{u}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}V. $$

Finally, by Poincare’s inequality and Young’s inequality with $\delta>0$ , it holds

$$ C_{m}\|\nabla\bm{u}\|_{L_{2}}\|\nabla\bm{J}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq\left(\frac{C_{m}^{2}C_{\mathrm{P}}^{2}}{4\delta}\mbox{{Ek}}^{(\gamma-1)}+\delta\mbox{{Ek}}^{(1-\gamma)}\|\nabla^{2}\bm{u}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\right)\|\nabla\bm{J}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}. $$

Combining Proposition 6.1 with (6.40), (6.44), (6.46) and (6.47), it follows that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int|\bm{J}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}V\leq \displaystyle\Bigg(C_{n}\mbox{{Ra}}\,\|\overline{\nabla\times\nabla\times T\bm{e}_{z}}\|_{L^{2}}+\mbox{{Ek}}^{1-\gamma}\mbox{{Ra}}^{2}\,\|\nabla\times\overline{\nabla\times\nabla\times T\bm{e}_{z}}\|_{L^{2}}^{2} \displaystyle+\frac{C_{m}^{2}C_{\mathrm{P}}^{2}}{4\delta}\mbox{{Ek}}^{(\gamma-1)}-\frac{1}{\mbox{{Rm}}}\Bigg)\int|\nabla\bm{J}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}V \displaystyle+\frac{\mbox{{Ek}}}{\Lambda}\left(\frac{\delta\Lambda\|\nabla\bm{J}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{\mbox{{Ek}}^{\gamma}}+\frac{\mbox{{Ek}}^{\gamma}}{4\Lambda\|\nabla\bm{J}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}-1\right)\int|\nabla^{2}\bm{u}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}V. $$

Observe that the non-trivial choice of $\gamma$ which will give an analogous result for the inviscid case where $Ek\to 0$ is of $0<\gamma<1$ . Growth of magnetic enstrophy requires that the expression in the parentheses is nonnegative. Indeed, if the second parentheses in (6.48) is positive, with

$$ x=\frac{4\Lambda\|\nabla\bm{J}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{\mbox{{Ek}}^{\gamma}}, $$

we get

$$ \frac{\delta x}{4}+\frac{1}{x}-1>0. $$

Solving for $x$ gives

$$ x>\frac{2}{\delta}(1+\sqrt{1-\delta}),\quad\text{or}\quad x<\frac{2}{\delta}(1-\sqrt{1-\delta}). $$

For $\delta\geq 1$ , the condition is true for all $x$ . For $\delta<1$ , a simple, though weaker, condition is that $\sqrt{1-\delta}\geq 1-\delta$ . This gives

$$ x>\frac{4}{\delta}-2,\quad\text{or}\quad x<2. $$

The result is exactly the choice of $\delta$ such that

$$ \frac{C_{m}^{2}C_{\mathrm{P}}^{2}\,\mbox{{Ek}}^{(\gamma-1)}}{4\delta}=\frac{1}{2\mbox{{Rm}}}. $$

∎

#### Proof of Lemma 6.2.

Let us rewrite the two terms. For the first term, because $\bm{B}$ and $\bm{J}$ are divergence free, it follows that pointwise

$$ \bm{J}\times\nabla^{2}\bm{B}=-\bm{J}\times(\nabla\times\bm{J})=(\bm{J}\cdot\nabla)\bm{J}-\frac{1}{2}\nabla|\bm{J}|^{2}. $$

Integrating by parts against divergence-free $\bm{u}$ yields and using the boundary conditions on $\bm{J}$ gives

$$ \displaystyle\int\bm{u}\cdot(\bm{J}\times\nabla^{2}\bm{B})\,\mathrm{d}V \displaystyle=\int\bm{u}\cdot\left(\bm{J}\cdot\nabla\right)\bm{J}\,\mathrm{d}V \displaystyle=\int\bm{u}\cdot(\nabla\cdot\left(\bm{J}\otimes\bm{J}\right))\,\mathrm{d}V=-\int\nabla\bm{u}:(\bm{J}\otimes\bm{J})\,\mathrm{d}V. $$

For the second term, integration by parts yields

$$ \displaystyle-2\int\bm{u}\cdot(\nabla\cdot(\bm{J}\times\nabla\bm{B}))\,\mathrm{d}V \displaystyle=2\int\nabla\bm{u}:(\bm{J}\times\nabla\bm{B})\,\mathrm{d}V. $$

Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\int\bm{u}\cdot(\bm{J}\times\nabla^{2}\bm{B}-2\nabla\cdot(\bm{J}\times\nabla\bm{B}))\,\mathrm{d}V \displaystyle=\int\nabla\bm{u}:(2\bm{J}\times\nabla\bm{B}-\bm{J}\otimes\bm{J})\,\mathrm{d}V \displaystyle\leq 3\int|\nabla\bm{u}||\nabla\bm{B}||\bm{J}|\,\mathrm{d}V. $$

Hölder’s inequality implies

$$ \int|\nabla\bm{u}||\nabla\bm{B}||\bm{J}|\,\mathrm{d}V\leq\|\nabla\bm{u}\|_{L^{2}}\|\nabla\bm{B}\|_{L^{3}}\|\bm{J}\|_{L^{6}}, $$

and by $L^{p}$ interpolation we can write

$$ \|\nabla\bm{B}\|_{L^{3}}\leq\|\nabla\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}}^{1/2}\|\nabla\bm{B}\|_{L^{6}}^{1/2}. $$

Using the Sobolev estimate for $\nabla\bm{B}$ and $\bm{J}$ ,

$$ \|\nabla\bm{B}\|_{L^{6}}\leq C_{\mathrm{S}}\|\nabla\nabla\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}}=C_{\mathrm{S}}\|\nabla\bm{J}\|_{L^{2}}, $$

and the Poincaré inequality, we conclude that

$$ \int|\nabla\bm{u}||\nabla\bm{B}||\bm{J}|\,\mathrm{d}V\leq C_{\mathrm{S}}^{3/2}C_{\mathrm{P}}^{1/2}\|\nabla\bm{u}\|_{L^{2}}\|\nabla\bm{J}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}. $$

Therefore, setting $C_{m}=3C_{\mathrm{P}}^{1/2}C_{\mathrm{S}}^{3/2}$ completes the proof. ∎

## 7. Proof of Theorems: Thermal Estimates

### 7.1. Inviscid Case

We first identify radii of the absorbing balls for temperature quantities which control the quantities of interest in section 3. The results are obtained by a standard use of energy methods on (2.1e).

#### Proposition 7.1.

Suppose $T$ satisfies the temperature equation and homogeneous isothermal boundary conditions, for divergence-free $\bm{u}$ satisfying no-penetration boundary conditions. Let $2\leq p<\infty$ and suppose that $Q\in L^{p}$ is time independent. Then,

$$ \limsup_{t\to\infty}\|T(t)\|_{L^{p}}\leq\frac{p^{2}\|Q\|_{L^{p}}}{4\pi^{2}(p-1)}. $$

#### Proof.

Multiplying (2.1e) by $|T|^{p-2}T$ where $p\geq 2$ , integrating over the domain and using the boundary conditions, incompressibility and integrating by parts gives

$$ \frac{1}{p}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int|T|^{p}\,\mathrm{d}V=\frac{1}{\mbox{{Pe}}}\int Q\,|T|^{p-2}T\,\mathrm{d}V-\frac{1}{\mbox{{Pe}}}\int\nabla(|T|^{p-2}T)\cdot\nabla T\,\mathrm{d}V. $$

The dissipative term can be simplified by rearranging and using the Poincaré inequality,

$$ \displaystyle\int\nabla(|T|^{p-2}T)\nabla T\,\mathrm{d}V \displaystyle=(p-1)\int|\nabla T|^{2}T^{p-2}\mathrm{d}V=(p-1)\int|T^{p/2-1}\nabla T|^{2}\mathrm{d}V \displaystyle=\frac{4(p-1)}{p^{2}}\int|\nabla|T|^{p/2}|^{2}\mathrm{d}V\geq\frac{4\pi^{2}(p-1)}{p^{2}}\int|T|^{p}\mathrm{d}V. $$

Substituting (7.2) into (7.1), and using Hölders inequality on the source term gives

$$ \frac{1}{p}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\|T\|_{L^{p}}^{p}\leq\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{p}}}{\mbox{{Pe}}}\|T\|_{L^{p}}^{(p-1)}-\frac{4\pi^{2}(p-1)}{\mbox{{Pe}}\,p^{2}}\|T\|_{L^{p}}^{p}. $$

Differentiating the left hand side and dividing through by $\|T\|_{L^{p}}^{(p-1)}$ , we get

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\|T\|_{L^{p}}\leq\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{p}}}{\mbox{{Pe}}}-\frac{4\pi^{2}(p-1)}{\mbox{{Pe}}\,p^{2}}\|T\|_{L^{p}}. $$

Using Gronwall’s lemma finally gives the desired result

$$ \displaystyle\|T(t)\|_{L^{p}}\leq \displaystyle\|T(0)\|_{L^{p}}\exp\left\{-\frac{4\pi^{2}(p-1)t}{\mbox{{Pe}}\,p^{2}}\right\} \displaystyle+\frac{p^{2}\|Q\|_{L^{p}}}{4\pi^{2}(p-1)}\left(1-\exp\left\{-\frac{4\pi^{2}(p-1)t}{\mbox{{Pe}}\,p^{2}}\right\}\right), $$

after taking the limit superior as time $t\to\infty$ . ∎

#### Proposition 7.2.

Suppose $T$ satisfies the temperature equation and isothermal boundary conditions, for divergence-free $\bm{u}$ satisfying no-penetration boundary conditions. Suppose that $Q\in H^{1}$ is time independent. Let,

$$ U_{\infty}Pe<\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{1+\pi^{2}}}, $$

then,

$$ \limsup_{t\to\infty}\|\nabla^{2}T(t)\|_{L^{2}}\leq\left(\frac{U_{\infty}\mbox{{Pe}}\,\|Q\|_{H^{1}}}{\pi-\sqrt{1+\pi^{2}}U_{\infty}\mbox{{Pe}}}+\|Q\|_{L^{2}}\right). $$

#### Proof.

Define

$$ \vartheta:=\nabla^{2}T+Q. $$

Tracing (2.1e) to the boundaries $S_{\pm}$ , the isothermal boundary conditions for $T$ and no-penetration boundary conditions for $\bm{u}$ yield

$$ \vartheta|_{\,S_{\pm}}=\left(\nabla^{2}T+Q\right)|_{\,S_{\pm}}=0. $$

Because $Q$ is time independent, applying the Laplacian to (2.1e) gives

$$ \partial_{t}\vartheta+\nabla^{2}(\bm{u}\cdot\nabla T)=\frac{1}{\mbox{{Pe}}}\nabla^{2}\vartheta. $$

Multiplying (7.8) by $\vartheta$ , integrating over $V$ , and using (7.7), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\|\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}^{2} \displaystyle=-\int\vartheta\nabla^{2}(\bm{u}\cdot\nabla T),\mathrm{d}V+\frac{1}{\mbox{{Pe}}}\int\vartheta\nabla^{2}\vartheta\mathrm{d}V \displaystyle=\int\nabla\vartheta\cdot\nabla(\bm{u}\cdot\nabla T)\mathrm{d}V-\frac{1}{\mbox{{Pe}}}\|\nabla\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}. $$

Expanding the nonlinear term gives

$$ \displaystyle\int\nabla\vartheta\cdot\nabla(\bm{u}\cdot\nabla T)\mathrm{d}V \displaystyle=\int\nabla\vartheta\cdot(\nabla\bm{u})^{T}\nabla T\mathrm{d}V+\int\nabla\vartheta\cdot(\bm{u}\cdot\nabla)\nabla T\mathrm{d}V. $$

By Hölder’s inequality,

$$ \displaystyle\left|\int\nabla\vartheta\cdot\nabla(\bm{u}\cdot\nabla T)\mathrm{d}V\right| \displaystyle\leq(\|\bm{u}\|_{L^{3}}\|\nabla\nabla T\|_{L^{6}}+\|\nabla\bm{u}\|_{L^{2}}\|\nabla T\|_{L^{\infty}})\|\nabla\vartheta\|_{L^{2}} $$

Next, given that $C_{\infty}$ and $C_{\mathrm{S}}$ be admissible Sobolev–elliptic constants satisfying

$$ \|\nabla T\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C_{\infty}\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{H^{1}},\qquad\|\nabla\nabla T\|_{L^{6}}\leq C_{\mathrm{S},0}\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{H^{1}}. $$

Thus (7.11) and (7.12) motivate the definition (4.2) such that

$$ \left|\int\nabla\vartheta\cdot\nabla(\bm{u}\cdot\nabla T)\mathrm{d}V\right|\leq U_{\infty}\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{H^{1}}\|\nabla\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}. $$

On the other hand, by applying the Poincaré inequality to the definition of $\vartheta$ ,

$$ \|\nabla^{2}T\|_{H^{1}}\leq\left(1+\frac{1}{\pi^{2}}\right)^{1/2}\|\nabla\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}+\|Q\|_{H^{1}}. $$

Therefore, from (7.13),

$$ \left|\int\nabla\vartheta\cdot\nabla(\bm{u}\cdot\nabla T)\mathrm{d}V\right|\leq\left(1+\frac{1}{\pi^{2}}\right)^{1/2}U_{\infty}\|\nabla\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+U_{\infty}\|Q\|_{H^{1}}\|\nabla\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}. $$

Combining (7.9) and (7.15) yields

$$ \frac{1}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\|\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq-\gamma\|\nabla\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+U_{\infty}\|Q\|_{H^{1}}\|\nabla\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}. $$

where

$$ \gamma=\frac{1}{\mbox{{Pe}}}-\left(1+\frac{1}{\pi^{2}}\right)^{1/2}U_{\infty} $$

For any $\varepsilon>0$ , Young’s inequality gives

$$ U_{\infty}\|Q\|_{H^{1}}\|\nabla\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}\leq\varepsilon\gamma\|\nabla\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\frac{U_{\infty}^{2}\|Q\|_{H^{1}}^{2}}{4\varepsilon\gamma}. $$

Substituting (7.18) into (7.16) with $\varepsilon=1/2$ gives

$$ \frac{1}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\|\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq-\frac{1}{2}\gamma\|\nabla\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\frac{U_{\infty}^{2}\|Q\|_{H^{1}}^{2}}{2\gamma}. $$

Using Poincaré’s inequality again,

$$ \|\nabla\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\geq\pi^{2}\|\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}, $$

we obtain

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\|\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq-\gamma\pi^{2}\|\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\frac{U_{\infty}^{2}\|Q\|_{H^{1}}^{2}}{\gamma}. $$

Gronwall’s inequality gives

$$ \displaystyle\|\vartheta(t)\|_{2}^{2} \displaystyle\leq\|\vartheta_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\exp\{-\gamma\pi^{2}t\}+\frac{U_{\infty}^{2}\|Q\|_{H^{1}}^{2}}{\gamma^{2}\pi^{2}}\left(1-\exp\{-\gamma\pi^{2}t\}\right). $$

Therefore,

$$ \limsup_{t\to\infty}\|\vartheta(t)\|_{L^{2}}\leq\frac{U_{\infty}\|Q\|_{H^{1}}}{\gamma\pi}. $$

Finally, we have

$$ \|\nabla^{2}T\|_{L^{2}}\leq\|\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}+\|Q\|_{L^{2}}. $$

Combining (7.23) and (7.24) gives

$$ \limsup_{t\to\infty}\|\nabla^{2}T(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq\left(\frac{U_{\infty}\|Q\|_{H^{1}}}{\gamma\pi}+\|Q\|_{L^{2}}\right)^{2}. $$

This proves the result. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 4.1.

In fact

$$ \|\nabla_{x,y}\overline{T}\|_{L^{3}}=\|\overline{\nabla_{x,y}T}\|_{L^{3}}\leq b_{3}\|\nabla_{x,y}T\|_{L^{3}}\leq b_{3}\|\nabla T\|_{L^{3}} $$

where $b_{3}$ is the constant given in Lemma 7.3. Then, by $L^{p}$ interpolation we have that

$$ \|\nabla T\|_{L^{3}}\leq\|\nabla T\|_{L^{2}}^{1/2}\|\nabla T\|_{L^{6}}^{1/2}. $$

Then, using the temperature boundary conditions, we can integrate by parts and use the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to write that

$$ \int|\nabla T|^{2}\mathrm{d}V=-\int T\nabla^{2}T\mathrm{d}V\leq\|T\|_{L^{2}}\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{L^{2}}. $$

Using (7.28) and the Sobolev embedding $H^{1}\hookrightarrow L^{6}$ gives that

$$ \|\nabla T\|_{L^{3}}\leq C_{\mathrm{S}}^{1/2}\|T\|_{L^{2}}^{1/4}\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{L^{2}}^{3/4}. $$

Taking long-time limit, we have that

$$ \|T\|_{L^{2}}\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{L^{2}}\leq\limsup_{t\to\infty}\left(\|T\|_{L^{2}}\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{L^{2}}\right)\leq\left(\limsup_{t\to\infty}\|T\|_{L^{2}}\right)\left(\limsup_{t\to\infty}\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{L^{2}}\right). $$

Therefore, using the bound on $\nabla^{2}T\in L^{2}$ from Proposition 7.2 and on $T\in L^{2}$ from Proposition 7.1 with $p=2$ , the result follows.

∎

#### Proof of Theorem 4.3.

We shall establish

$$ \|\nabla_{x,y}^{2}\overline{T}\|_{L^{\infty}_{z}L^{2}_{x,y}}\leq\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{L^{2}} $$

and the claim follows from an application of Proposition 7.2.

A basic property of the integral is

$$ \left\|\int_{0}^{z}\nabla_{x,y}^{2}T(z^{\prime})\,dz^{\prime}\right\|_{L^{2}_{x,y}}\leq\int_{0}^{z}\|\nabla_{x,y}^{2}T(z^{\prime})\|_{L^{2}_{x,y}}dz^{\prime}. $$

Taking the supremum in $z$ , it holds

$$ \|\nabla_{x,y}^{2}\overline{T}\|_{L^{\infty}_{z}L^{2}_{x,y}}\leq\|\nabla_{x,y}^{2}T\|_{L^{2}}. $$

Now we establish

$$ \|\nabla_{x,y}^{2}T\|_{L^{2}}\leq\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{L^{2}}. $$

Observe that

$$ \langle\nabla^{2}T,\nabla^{2}T\rangle=\langle\nabla_{x,y}^{2}T,\nabla_{x,y}^{2}T\rangle+2\langle\partial_{z}^{2}T,\nabla_{x,y}^{2}T\rangle+\langle\partial_{z}^{2}T,\partial_{z}^{2}T\rangle. $$

The cross term we may integrate by parts in $dz$ ,

$$ \langle\partial_{z}^{2}T,\nabla_{x,y}^{2}T\rangle=-\langle\partial_{z}T,\nabla_{x,y}^{2}\partial_{z}T\rangle\pm\int(\partial_{z}T)\nabla_{x,y}^{2}T\,dS_{\pm}. $$

For isothermal boundary conditions $\nabla_{x,y}^{2}T$ vanishes on the boundary $S_{\pm}$ . Therefore we may further integrate by parts the cross term in $\mathrm{d}S$ such that

$$ \langle\partial_{z}^{2}T,\nabla_{x,y}^{2}T\rangle=\langle\nabla_{x,y}\partial_{z}T,T\partial_{z}T\rangle\geq 0. $$

This establishes estimate (7.34), and the result follows. ∎

#### Remark 7.1.

For Rayleigh–Bénard convection where the boundary conditions are inhomogeneous, one may consider perturbations about the conductive state. One then finds an evolution equation equivalent to the above, and the results hold with $u_{z}$ in place of $Q$ .

### 7.2. Viscous Case

We first state and prove two lemmas that estimate norms of primitive variables, that are used in the results of section 4.

#### Lemma 7.3.

Let $1\leq p<\infty$ and $\bm{f}\in L^{p}(\mathrm{d}V)$ . Then,

$$ \|\overline{f}\|_{L^{p}}\leq b_{p}\|f\|_{L^{p}}, $$

where

$$ b_{p}=\begin{cases}1&p=1,\\
\frac{p\sin(\pi/p)}{\pi(p-1)^{1/p}}&p>1.\end{cases} $$

#### Proof.

If one considers $\overline{\,\cdot\,\vphantom{i}}$ as an operator on $L^{p}_{z}$ , it is in fact Volterra and has the operator norm $b_{p}$ per [BS02, Theorem 3.1]. Noting that $L^{p}(dV)=L^{p}_{x,y}L^{p}_{z}$ , the result follows. ∎

#### Lemma 7.4.

Let $f\in H^{2}$ and suppose that $f\,|_{\,S_{\pm}}=0$ . Then

$$ \|\nabla\nabla_{x,y}\overline{f}\|_{L^{2}}\leq(C_{\mathrm{P}}+b_{2})\|\nabla^{2}f\|_{L^{2}}. $$

#### Proof.

Because $\nabla_{x,y}f$ vanishes at the boundary, it holds

$$ \nabla\nabla_{x,y}\overline{f}=(\nabla_{x,y}\nabla_{x,y}\overline{f},\nabla_{x,y}f). $$

We have the identity

$$ \|\nabla_{x,y}\nabla_{x,y}\overline{f}\|_{L^{2}}=\|\overline{\nabla_{x,y}^{2}f}\|_{L^{2}} $$

Therefore, by Lemma 7.3 and Lemma 5.5

$$ \displaystyle\|\nabla\nabla_{x,y}\overline{f}\|_{L^{2}} \displaystyle\leq\|\overline{\nabla_{x,y}^{2}f}\|_{L^{2}}+\|\nabla_{x,y}f\|_{L^{2}} \displaystyle\leq(b_{2}+C_{\mathrm{P}})\|\nabla_{x,y}^{2}f\|_{L^{2}} $$

With the previous estimate (7.34), we are done. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 4.5.

Following the proof of Theorem 3.5 utilising the poloidal-toroidal decomposition estimates Propositions 5.3 and 5.4, we find that dynamo action requires that

$$ \mbox{{Ra}}\,A_{2}\|\nabla^{2}_{x,y}\overline{T}\|_{L^{\infty_{z}}L_{x,y}^{2}}+\mbox{{Ra}}^{2}\,\mbox{{Ek}}^{1-\gamma}\|\nabla\nabla_{x,y}\overline{T}\|^{2}_{L^{2}}\,\geq\frac{1}{\mbox{{Rm}}} $$

or

$$ 4\Lambda\int|\nabla\bm{B}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}V\leq\mbox{{Ek}}^{\gamma}. $$

Applying the estimate (7.31) and Lemma 7.3, the first requirement is

$$ \mbox{{Ra}}\,A_{2}\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{L^{2}}+\mbox{{Ra}}^{2}\,\mbox{{Ek}}^{1-\gamma}C_{\mathrm{P},2}^{2}\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\,\geq\frac{1}{\mbox{{Rm}}}. $$

Defining $x=\mbox{{Ra}}_{\nu}\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{L^{2}}$ and using relation (4.8) of the classical Rayleigh number $\mbox{{Ra}}_{\nu}$ , the requirement for dynamo action is simply

$$ C_{\mathrm{P},2}^{2}\frac{\mbox{{Ek}}^{3-\gamma}}{\mbox{{Pe}}^{2}}x^{2}+A_{2}\frac{\mbox{{Ek}}}{\mbox{{Pe}}}x-\frac{1}{\mbox{{Rm}}}\geq 0. $$

Solving the quadratic furnishes the result. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 4.6.

First, assume that $Q=Q(z)$ and let $\tau$ be the conductive state solving (4.12). The evolution equation for $\theta=T-\tau$ is

$$ \partial_{t}\theta+\bm{u}\cdot\nabla\theta+u_{z}\tau^{\prime}=Pe^{-1}\nabla^{2}\theta $$

and the perturbation vanishes at the boundary,

$$ \theta=0\quad\text{on }S_{\pm}. $$

Testing (7.43) against $-\nabla^{2}\theta$ and integrating gives

$$ \frac{1}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int|\nabla\theta|^{2}\mathrm{d}V=-Pe^{-1}\int|\nabla^{2}\theta|^{2}\mathrm{d}V+\int\nabla^{2}\theta\,\bm{u}\cdot\nabla\theta\,\mathrm{d}V+\int\tau^{\prime}u_{z}\nabla^{2}\theta\,\mathrm{d}V. $$

By Hölder’s inequality and the estimate

$$ \|\nabla\theta\|_{L^{6}}\leq C_{\mathrm{S},0}\|\nabla^{2}\theta\|_{L^{2}} $$

we get

$$ \left|\int\nabla^{2}\theta\,\bm{u}\cdot\nabla\theta\,\mathrm{d}V\right|\leq\|\bm{u}\|_{L^{3}}\|\nabla\theta\|_{L^{6}}\|\nabla^{2}\theta\|_{L^{2}}\leq C_{\mathrm{S},0}\|\bm{u}\|_{L^{3}}\|\nabla^{2}\theta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}. $$

For the final term in (7.45), using Cauchy-Schwarz in the horizontal directions and then Hölders in $z$ gives,

$$ \displaystyle\left|\int\tau^{\prime}u_{z}\nabla^{2}\theta\mathrm{d}V\right|\leq\left|\int^{1}_{0}\tau^{\prime}\|u_{z}\|_{L^{2}_{x,y}}\|\nabla^{2}\theta\|_{L^{2}_{x,y}}\mathrm{d}z\right|\leq\|\tau^{\prime}\|_{L^{2}_{z}}\|u_{z}\|_{L^{\infty}_{z}L^{2}_{x,y}}\|\nabla^{2}\theta\|_{L^{2}}. $$

Since $u_{z}=0$ on $S_{\pm}$ , exploiting both boundary conditions,

$$ \displaystyle u_{z}=(1-z)\int^{z}_{0}\partial_{z^{\prime}}u_{z}\mathrm{d}z^{\prime}-z\int^{1}_{z}\partial_{z^{\prime}}u_{z}\mathrm{d}z^{\prime}=\int^{1}_{0}\xi_{z}(z^{\prime})\partial_{z^{\prime}}u_{z}\mathrm{d}z^{\prime} $$

where $\xi_{z}$ is defined as

$$ \xi_{z}(z^{\prime})=\begin{cases}1-z,&0\leq z^{\prime}\leq z,\\
-z,&z\leq z^{\prime}\leq 1.\end{cases} $$

Then, taking the horizontal $L^{2}$ norm of $u_{z}$ , using Cauchy-Schwarz in $z$ and evaluating the integral of $|\xi_{z}(z^{\prime})|^{2}$ gives

$$ \displaystyle\|u_{z}\|_{L^{2}_{x,y}} \displaystyle=\left\|\int^{1}_{0}\xi_{z}(z^{\prime})\partial_{z^{\prime}}u_{z}\mathrm{d}z^{\prime}\right\|_{L^{2}_{x,y}}\leq\|\xi_{z}\|_{L^{2}_{z}}\|\partial_{z}u_{z}\|_{L^{2}} \displaystyle\leq\|\xi_{z}\|_{L^{2}_{z}}\|\nabla\bm{u}\|_{L^{2}}=\sqrt{z(1-z)}\|\nabla\bm{u}\|_{L^{2}}. $$

Taking the supremum yields $\|u_{z}\|_{L^{\infty}_{z}L^{2}_{x,y}}\leq\frac{1}{2}\|\nabla\bm{u}\|_{L^{2}}$ . Substituting this bound into (7.48), multiplying through by $Pe$ and using Young’s inequality gives

$$ \displaystyle Pe\left|\int\tau^{\prime}u_{z}\nabla^{2}\theta\mathrm{d}V\right| \displaystyle\leq Pe\|\tau^{\prime}\|_{L^{2}_{z}}\|\nabla\bm{u}\|_{L^{2}}\|\nabla^{2}\theta\|_{L^{2}} \displaystyle\leq Ek(1-x)\int|\nabla\bm{u}|^{2}\mathrm{d}V+\frac{Pe^{2}\|\tau^{\prime}\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{z}}}{4Ek(1-x)}\int|\nabla^{2}\theta|^{2}\mathrm{d}V. $$

Substituting (7.52) and (7.47) into (7.45) gives

$$ \displaystyle\frac{Pe}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int|\nabla\theta|^{2}\mathrm{d}V\leq \displaystyle\left(-1+C_{\mathrm{S},0}Pe\|\bm{u}\|_{L^{3}}+\frac{Pe^{2}\|\tau^{\prime}\|_{L^{2}_{z}}^{2}}{4Ek(1-x)}\right)\int|\nabla^{2}\theta|^{2}\mathrm{d}V \displaystyle+Ek(1-x)\int|\nabla\bm{u}|^{2}\mathrm{d}V $$

Next, testing the momentum equation (2.1a) against $\bm{u}$ and combining the result with $\bm{B}$ tested against the induction equation (2.1c) gives

$$ \frac{1}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int|\bm{B}|^{2}\mathrm{d}V=\frac{Ra}{\Lambda}\int u_{z}\theta\,\mathrm{d}V-\frac{Ek}{\Lambda}\int|\nabla\bm{u}|^{2}\mathrm{d}V-Rm^{-1}\int|\nabla\bm{B}|^{2}\mathrm{d}V. $$

For the production term, we shall use the previous estimate (6.10)

$$ \left|\int u_{z}\theta\,\mathrm{d}V\right|\leq\Lambda A_{p}\|\nabla_{x,y}\overline{\theta}\|_{L^{p}}\int|\nabla\bm{B}|^{2}\mathrm{d}V+Ek\|\nabla\nabla_{x,y}\overline{T}\|_{L^{2}}\|\nabla\bm{u}\|_{L^{2}} $$

Applying Lemma 7.4, estimate 7.55 and Young’s inequality with $x\in(0,1)$ , gives

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int|\bm{B}|^{2}\mathrm{d}V\leq \displaystyle\,(Ra\,A_{p}\|\nabla_{x,y}\overline{T}\|_{L^{p}}-Rm^{-1})\int|\nabla\bm{B}|^{2}\mathrm{d}V-\frac{Ek}{\Lambda}(1-x)\int|\nabla\bm{u}|^{2}\mathrm{d}V \displaystyle+\frac{C^{2}_{\mathrm{P},2}Ra^{2}Ek}{4\Lambda x}\int|\nabla^{2}\theta|^{2}\mathrm{d}V, $$

where $C_{\mathrm{P},2}=C_{\mathrm{P}}+b_{2}$ .

Next we form the equation for $\mathcal{E}=\Lambda\|\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+Pe\|\nabla\theta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}$ . Combining (7.53) with $\Lambda$ multiplying (7.56) cancels the terms proportional to $Ek(1-x)\|\nabla\bm{u}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}$ and gives

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{E}}{\mathrm{d}t}\leq~ \displaystyle\Lambda(Ra\,A_{p}\|\nabla_{x,y}\overline{T}\|_{L^{p}}-Rm^{-1})\int|\nabla\bm{B}|^{2}\mathrm{d}V \displaystyle+Pe\left(\frac{C^{2}_{\mathrm{P},2}Ra^{2}Ek}{4xPe}+\frac{Pe\|\tau^{\prime}\|_{L^{2}_{z}}^{2}}{4Ek(1-x)}-Pe^{-1}+C_{\mathrm{S},0}\|\bm{u}\|_{L^{3}}\right)\int|\nabla^{2}\theta|^{2}\mathrm{d}V, $$

For $a,b\geq 0$ ,

$$ \inf_{0<x<1}\left(\frac{a}{x}+\frac{b}{1-x}\right)=(\sqrt{a}+\sqrt{b})^{2}. $$

Therefore, minimising the second bracket in (7.57) gives

$$ \left(\frac{C_{\mathrm{P},2}\,Ra\sqrt{Ek}}{2\sqrt{Pe}}+\frac{\sqrt{Pe}\|\tau^{\prime}\|_{L^{2}_{z}}}{2\sqrt{Ek}}\right)^{2}-Pe^{-1}+C_{\mathrm{S},0}\|\bm{u}\|_{L^{3}}. $$

Consequently, non-decay of $\mathcal{E}$ requires either of the two brackets in eq. 7.57 to be non-negative. ∎

## 8. Discussion

This work establishes necessary conditions for the instantaneous growth of magnetic energy in rotating convection. We consider the magnetohydrodynamic model of J. B. Taylor for the Earth’s outer core, and its viscous extension. We prove antidynamo theorems: quantitative conditions that are necessary for magnetic energy growth in rapidly rotating convection. Our analysis identifies the horizontal variation of the vertically integrated temperature as the quantity controlling the necessary conditions for dynamo action. The bounds therefore extend the logic of classical kinematic antidynamo estimates to a fully nonlinear setting.

A finding of our work is the significance of the Archimedean velocity $\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}$ , i.e., the buoyancy-driven part of the flow. In particular, magnetic energy growth requires, for $3\leq p\leq\infty$

$$ \mbox{{Rm}}\,A_{p}\|\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}\|_{L^{p}}\geq 1, $$

where $A_{p}$ is an explicit constant given in Appendix A. The constraint holds for Taylor’s model and for the inertialess model with finite viscosity $\mbox{{Ek}}>0$ . The precise statements are Theorems 3.2 and 3.6. We refine our bound via poloidal-toroidal decomposition to replace $L^{p}$ with $L^{\infty}_{z}\dot{H}^{1}_{x,y}$ in the above constraint.

### 8.1. Taylor Dynamo

Taylor’s constraint complicates the analysis of the inertialess model. The production of magnetic energy in its basic form depends on the vertical (poloidal) component of the flow $u_{z}$ ; however, by identities from Taylor’s constraint, the magnetic energy production is driven by a purely horizontal (toroidal) part of the flow

$$ \bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}=\mbox{{Ra}}\,\nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\overline{T}. $$

Crucially, our results are independent of the geostrophic component of the flow which is typically difficult to compute. The precise statement is Theorem 3.1.

Our analysis without nondimensionalising yields the requirement for dynamo action

$$ \mbox{{Ra}}_{T}=\frac{g\alpha d^{1-\frac{3}{p}}\|\nabla_{x,y}\overline{T}\|_{L^{p}}}{2\Omega\eta}\geq A^{-1}_{p}. $$

Therefore, for flows normalised by the temperature scale given by a ( dimensional) $\|\nabla_{x,y}\overline{T}\|_{L^{p}}$ , a lower bound for Ra is $A^{-1}_{p}$ . In terms of a classical Rayleigh number $\mbox{{Ra}}_{\eta}$ our constraint for dynamo action has the form

$$ Ra_{\eta}\gtrsim q^{-1}Ek_{\eta}^{-1}. $$

In long-time convection, the implicit constant in this requirement depends on the radii of absorbing balls. For uniform internal heating, see Corollaries 4.2 and 4.4.

### 8.2. Viscous Dynamo

At finite Ekman number $\mbox{{Ek}}>0$ , viscosity removes the computational difficulties associated with the inviscid model. Our requirements for dynamo action hold with viscous corrections which vanish as $\mbox{{Ek}}\to 0$ ; our dynamo criteria are not based on singular properties of Taylor’s constraint.

The viscous corrections are explicitly given in Theorem 3.5. Writing Theorem 3.5 in terms of a classical Rayleigh number $Ra_{\nu}$ , our requirement for dynamo action takes the form

$$ Ra_{\nu}\gtrsim PeEk^{-3/2}. $$

In addition to the magnetic energy, in Theorem 3.7 we provide a necessary condition for the growth of magnetic enstrophy, given Rm is sufficiently small. The magnetic energy and enstrophy growth conditions are complementary. If growth conditions of magnetic energy enstrophy are both not satisfied, then the magnetic field and its gradients must decay.

Our final result concerns the thermo-magnetic energy $\mathcal{E}=\Lambda\|\bm{B}\|_{2}^{2}+Pe\|\nabla\theta\|_{2}^{2}$ in Theorem 4.6. The conductive profile affects the second combined energy condition through $\|\tau^{\prime}\|_{L^{2}_{z}}$ , where the conductive state corresponds to $Q(z)=-\tau^{\prime\prime}(z)$ . For the combined energy to grow, at least one of two conditions must be satisfied. The first is the magnetic energy condition of Theorem 3.6. The second result arises from a balance of thermal diffusion against the advection of thermal gradients, the conductive gradient $\tau^{\prime}$ and the viscous dissipation. In the case of $Pe\sim Ek^{1/2}$ for $Ek\ll 1$ where $\mathcal{E}\to\Lambda\|\bm{B}\|^{2}_{2}$ and non-decay requires $Ra_{\nu}\gtrsim Ek^{-1}$ . For $Pe\sim 1$ and conductive states such that $\|\tau^{\prime}\|_{L^{2}_{z}}\mbox{{Ek}}^{-1/2}\ll 1$ , the non-decay requirement is $Ra_{\nu}\gtrsim Ek^{-3/2}$ as before. Such conductive states are generated by heating profiles $Q=Q(z)$ which are oscillatory or concentrated at the boundaries.

Unlike Taylor’s model, the viscous inertialess model permits the onset of convection from a conductive solution. In particular, there exists a critical Rayleigh number $Ra_{\nu}^{*}$ , above which the flow is linearly unstable to convection. At the onset of convection, for Elsasser numbers of $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon)$ , it is known that for boundary and internal heating, $Ra_{\nu}^{*}\sim Ek^{-4/3}$ [Cha53, Ars24]. For comparison, in the magnetostrophic limit where the Elsasser number is $\mathcal{O}(1)$ , of rotating convection subject to a vertical background magnetic field, $Ra_{\nu}^{*}\sim Ek^{-1}$ . This is not the self-consistent dynamo onset problem considered here, but provides a useful reference scaling. Indicative scalings are plotted in fig. 2 along with data from successful dynamo simulations in the plane layer.

### 8.3. Scope and Future Outlook

Several qualifications should be kept in mind when interpreting these results. First, our conditions are strictly necessary, but are not sufficient for dynamo action. A smooth solution to the inertialess models may continuously satisfy our constraints without exhibiting any magnetic energy growth. We impose strictly impenetrable, stress-free and ferromagnetic boundary conditions however several of our arguments apply to spherical domains, mutatis mutandis.

The numerical values of the thresholds use admissible rather than sharp constants (appendix A). The constants depend on the domain. The temperature absorbing radii introduce additional losses when the entire temperature gradient is estimated instead of its dynamically relevant horizontal structures. The bounds should consequently be regarded as quantitative but conservative. The results in section 3 can be applied to different equations governing the temperature, provided the buoyancy force retains the same structure. As such the results can apply to double-diffusive convection [HT81, Gar18]. An interesting application would be to alternative models like Maxwell-Cattaneo convection [HPE21], convection with anisotropic or nonlinear thermal diffusion, or anelastic convection [AJS05].

It would be useful to evaluate the necessary conditions using numerical dynamo solutions, both to measure the gap between the inequalities and observed onset and to identify which estimates produce the largest losses [JR00, HC16, CH17, HC19]. Finally, the study of magnetohydrodynamics with recent mathematical tools would be valuable, like methods for bounding the long-time averages of quantities, used to study turbulence [FAW22]. Establishing such long-time constraints would turn the instantaneous obstructions derived here into a nonlinear analogue of the classical antidynamo theory for sustained magnetic fields.

#### Proof of $C_{\mathrm{S}}$ .

Let $\bm{B}$ be horizontally periodic, solenoidal, and satisfy ferromagnetic boundary conditions in addition to net zero flux. Then the constant $C_{\mathrm{S}}$ appears in the inequality $\|\bm{B}\|_{L^{6}(V)}\leq C_{\mathrm{S}}\|\nabla\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}(V)}$ where $V=[0,L_{x}]\times[0,L_{y}]\times[0,1]$ .

We construct an extension to which the whole-space Sobolev inequality can be applied. Extend $B_{x}$ and $B_{y}$ oddly across $z=0,1$ , extend $B_{z}$ evenly across these planes, and extend all three components periodically in $x$ and $y$ . Denote the resulting field by $\widetilde{\bm{B}}$ . The boundary conditions ensure that $\widetilde{\bm{B}}\in H^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ .

Consider the enlarged box

$$ W=(-L_{x},2L_{x})\times(-L_{y},2L_{y})\times(-1,2). $$

Choose a product cutoff

$$ \eta(x,y,z)=\eta_{x}(x)\eta_{y}(y)\eta_{z}(z) $$

such that $\eta=1$ on $V$ , $\eta=0$ on $\partial W$ , and each factor varies linearly across the two adjoining cells.

To estimate the cutoff more precisely, set

$$ \ell_{x}=L_{x},\qquad\ell_{y}=L_{y},\qquad\ell_{z}=1. $$

For $i\in\{x,y,z\}$ and $s\in[0,\ell_{i}]$ , the three values of the corresponding cutoff factor satisfy

$$ \displaystyle\eta_{i}(s-\ell_{i}) \displaystyle=\frac{s}{\ell_{i}}, \displaystyle\eta_{i}(s) \displaystyle=1, \displaystyle\eta_{i}(s+\ell_{i}) \displaystyle=1-\frac{s}{\ell_{i}}. $$

Consequently,

$$ \sum_{j=-1}^{1}\eta_{i}(s+j\ell_{i})^{2}=1+\left(\frac{s}{\ell_{i}}\right)^{2}+\left(1-\frac{s}{\ell_{i}}\right)^{2}\leq 2, $$

and

$$ \sum_{j=-1}^{1}\left|\eta_{i}^{\prime}(s+j\ell_{i})\right|^{2}=\frac{2}{\ell_{i}^{2}}. $$

Set

$$ \bm{F}=\eta\widetilde{\bm{B}} $$

on $W$ , and extend $\bm{F}$ by zero outside $W$ . Then $\bm{F}\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3};\mathbb{R}^{3})$ and $\bm{F}=\bm{B}$ on $V$ . By the product rule,

$$ \nabla\bm{F}=\eta\nabla\widetilde{\bm{B}}+\widetilde{\bm{B}}\otimes\nabla\eta. $$

Decomposing $W$ into its $27$ translated and reflected copies of $V$ , and using (A.4) in each coordinate, gives

$$ \displaystyle\|\eta\nabla\widetilde{\bm{B}}\|_{L^{2}(W)}^{2} \displaystyle\leq 2^{3}\|\nabla\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}(V)}^{2} \displaystyle=8\|\nabla\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}(V)}^{2}. $$

Hence,

$$ \|\eta\nabla\widetilde{\bm{B}}\|_{L^{2}(W)}\leq 2\sqrt{2}\,\|\nabla\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}(V)}. $$

Similarly, since

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla\eta|^{2}={} \displaystyle|\eta_{x}^{\prime}|^{2}\eta_{y}^{2}\eta_{z}^{2}+\eta_{x}^{2}|\eta_{y}^{\prime}|^{2}\eta_{z}^{2} \displaystyle+\eta_{x}^{2}\eta_{y}^{2}|\eta_{z}^{\prime}|^{2}, $$

equations (A.4) and (A.5) imply

$$ \displaystyle\|\widetilde{\bm{B}}\otimes\nabla\eta\|_{L^{2}(W)}^{2}\leq{} \displaystyle 8\left(L_{x}^{-2}+L_{y}^{-2}+1\right)\|\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}(V)}^{2}. $$

Therefore,

$$ \|\widetilde{\bm{B}}\otimes\nabla\eta\|_{L^{2}(W)}\leq 2\sqrt{2}\,\sqrt{1+L_{x}^{-2}+L_{y}^{-2}}\,\|\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}(V)}. $$

Combining (A.6), (A.8), and (A.10), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\|\nabla\bm{F}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})}\leq 2\sqrt{2}\Bigl(\|\nabla\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}(V)} \displaystyle+\sqrt{1+L_{x}^{-2}+L_{y}^{-2}}\,\|\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}(V)}\Bigr). $$

Using the Poincaré inequality then gives

$$ \displaystyle\|\nabla\bm{F}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})}\leq 2\sqrt{2}\left(1+\frac{\sqrt{1+L_{x}^{-2}+L_{y}^{-2}}}{\lambda_{1}}\right)\|\nabla\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}(V)}. $$

Talenti’s sharp whole-space Sobolev inequality, applied to $|\bm{F}|$ , gives

$$ \|\bm{F}\|_{L^{6}(\mathbb{R}^{3})}\leq C_{3}\|\nabla|\bm{F}|\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})}\leq C_{3}\|\nabla\bm{F}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})}. $$

Since $\bm{F}=\bm{B}$ on $V$ , it follows from (A.12) that

$$ \|\bm{B}\|_{L^{6}(V)}\leq C_{\mathrm{S}}\|\nabla\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}(V)}, $$

with

$$ C_{\mathrm{S}}=2\sqrt{2}\,C_{3}\left(1+\frac{\sqrt{1+L_{x}^{-2}+L_{y}^{-2}}}{\lambda_{1}}\right). $$

∎

#### Remark A.1.

If a scalar or vector $f$ admits an $H^{1}_{loc}$ reflected extension to the enlarged domain and satisfies $\|f\|_{2}\leq\frac{1}{\lambda_{1}}\|\nabla f\|_{2}$ then the cutoff calculation proves $\|f\|_{6}\leq C_{6}\|\nabla f\|_{2}$ .

#### Remark A.2.

If a Poincaré inequality does not exist, as for the case of $\nabla^{2}T$ , then

$$ \|F\|_{6}\leq C_{\mathrm{S},0}\|F\|_{H^{1}} $$

where

$$ C_{\mathrm{S},0}:=2\sqrt{2}C_{3}\sqrt{2+L^{-2}_{x}+L^{-2}_{y}}. $$

#### Proof of $C_{\infty}$ .

Define the normalized eigenfunctions of the horizontally periodic Dirichlet Laplacian by

$$ e_{mnk}(x,y,z)=\left(\frac{2}{L_{x}L_{y}}\right)^{1/2}\exp\left[i\left(\frac{2\pi m}{L_{x}}x+\frac{2\pi n}{L_{y}}y\right)\right]\sin(k\pi z). $$

They satisfy

$$ -\Delta e_{mnk}=\lambda_{mnk}e_{mnk}. $$

Set $f=\Delta T$ . Writing

$$ T=\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\widehat{T}_{mnk}e_{mnk},\qquad f=\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\widehat{f}_{mnk}e_{mnk}, $$

Green’s identity, horizontal periodicity, and the conditions

$$ T=e_{mnk}=0\qquad\text{on }z=0,1 $$

give

$$ \widehat{f}_{mnk}=-\lambda_{mnk}\widehat{T}_{mnk}. $$

Notice that this identity does not require $f=\Delta T$ to vanish at the boundaries. Consequently,

$$ \nabla T=-\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{\widehat{f}_{mnk}}{\lambda_{mnk}}\nabla e_{mnk}. $$

Applying the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality with weights $1+\lambda_{mnk}-k^{2}\pi^{2}$ gives

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla T(x,y,z)|^{2}\leq \displaystyle\left[\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\bigl(1+\lambda_{mnk}-k^{2}\pi^{2}\bigr)|\widehat{f}_{mnk}|^{2}\right] \displaystyle\times\left[\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{|\nabla e_{mnk}(x,y,z)|^{2}}{\lambda_{mnk}^{\,2}\bigl(1+\lambda_{mnk}-k^{2}\pi^{2}\bigr)}\right]. $$

By Parseval’s identity in the horizontal variables and the completeness of the sine basis in the vertical variable,

$$ \sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\bigl(1+\lambda_{mnk}-k^{2}\pi^{2}\bigr)|\widehat{f}_{mnk}|^{2}=\|f\|_{2}^{2}+\|\nabla_{x,y}f\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|f\|_{H^{1}}^{2}. $$

Furthermore,

$$ |\nabla e_{mnk}(x,y,z)|^{2}=\frac{2}{L_{x}L_{y}}\left[\lambda_{mnk}-k^{2}\pi^{2}\sin^{2}(k\pi z)+k^{2}\pi^{2}\cos^{2}(k\pi z)\right]\leq\frac{2}{L_{x}L_{y}}\lambda_{mnk}. $$

It follows that

$$ |\nabla T(x,y,z)|^{2}\leq\frac{2}{L_{x}L_{y}}\left[\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\bigl(1+\lambda_{mnk}-k^{2}\pi^{2}\bigr)\lambda_{mnk}}\right]\|\Delta T\|_{H^{1}}^{2}. $$

Taking the supremum over $V$ proves the result. The series converges as the summand behaves as $\lambda_{mnk}^{-2}$ for large wavenumbers. This completes the proof. ∎

#### Proof of $C_{b}$ .

Set

$$ \alpha_{m}=\frac{2\pi m}{L_{x}},\qquad\beta_{n}=\frac{2\pi n}{L_{y}}. $$

The normalized eigenfunctions satisfying homogeneous Dirichlet conditions at $z=0,1$ are

$$ e^{D}_{mnk}(x,y,z)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{L_{x}L_{y}}}\,e^{\mathrm{i}(\alpha_{m}x+\beta_{n}y)}\sin(k\pi z),\qquad k\geq 1. $$

The normalized eigenfunctions satisfying homogeneous Neumann conditions are

$$ e^{N}_{mn0}(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{L_{x}L_{y}}}\,e^{\mathrm{i}(\alpha_{m}x+\beta_{n}y)} $$

for $k=0$ , and

$$ e^{N}_{mnk}(x,y,z)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{L_{x}L_{y}}}\,e^{\mathrm{i}(\alpha_{m}x+\beta_{n}y)}\cos(k\pi z),\qquad k\geq 1. $$

All these functions satisfy

$$ -\nabla^{2}e_{mnk}=\lambda_{mnk}e_{mnk}. $$

The horizontal components have Dirichlet expansions,

$$ B_{i}=\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\widehat{B}^{i}_{mnk}e^{D}_{mnk},\qquad i\in\{x,y\}, $$

whereas the vertical component has the Neumann expansion

$$ B_{z}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m,n\in\mathbb{Z},\ k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}\\
(m,n,k)\neq(0,0,0)\end{subarray}}\widehat{B}^{z}_{mnk}e^{N}_{mnk}. $$

The mode $(m,n,k)=(0,0,0)$ is absent because of the zero net-flux condition.

For either horizontal component, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives

$$ \displaystyle|B_{i}(x,y,z)|^{2} \displaystyle\leq\left[\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\bigl(1+\lambda_{mnk}+\lambda_{mnk}^{2}\bigr)|\widehat{B}^{i}_{mnk}|^{2}\right] \displaystyle\qquad\times\left[\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{|e^{D}_{mnk}(x,y,z)|^{2}}{1+\lambda_{mnk}+\lambda_{mnk}^{2}}\right]. $$

Since

$$ |e^{D}_{mnk}(x,y,z)|^{2}\leq\frac{2}{L_{x}L_{y}}, $$

the second factor in (A.31) is bounded by $C_{b}^{2}$ .

The same argument for the vertical component gives

$$ \displaystyle|B_{z}(x,y,z)|^{2} \displaystyle\leq\left[\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m,n\in\mathbb{Z},\ k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}\\
(m,n,k)\neq(0,0,0)\end{subarray}}\bigl(1+\lambda_{mnk}+\lambda_{mnk}^{2}\bigr)|\widehat{B}^{z}_{mnk}|^{2}\right] \displaystyle\qquad\times\left[\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m,n\in\mathbb{Z},\ k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}\\
(m,n,k)\neq(0,0,0)\end{subarray}}\frac{|e^{N}_{mnk}(x,y,z)|^{2}}{1+\lambda_{mnk}+\lambda_{mnk}^{2}}\right]. $$

The normalized Neumann eigenfunctions satisfy

$$ |e^{N}_{mnk}(x,y,z)|^{2}\leq\frac{2-\delta_{k0}}{L_{x}L_{y}}. $$

Consequently,

$$ |B_{i}(x,y,z)|^{2}\leq C_{b}^{2}\|B_{i}\|_{H^{2}_{\Delta}}^{2}\qquad\text{for }i\in\{x,y,z\}, $$

where

$$ \|\bm{B}\|^{2}_{H^{2}_{\Delta}}:=\|\bm{B}\|^{2}_{2}+\|\nabla\bm{B}\|_{2}^{2}+\|\nabla^{2}\bm{B}\|_{2} $$

Summing over the three components yields

$$ \displaystyle|\bm{B}(x,y,z)|^{2} \displaystyle=|B_{x}|^{2}+|B_{y}|^{2}+|B_{z}|^{2} \displaystyle\leq C_{b}^{2}\left(\|B_{x}\|_{H^{2}_{\Delta}}^{2}+\|B_{y}\|_{H^{2}_{\Delta}}^{2}+\|B_{z}\|_{H^{2}_{\Delta}}^{2}\right) \displaystyle=C_{b}^{2}\|\bm{B}\|_{H^{2}_{\Delta}}^{2}. $$

Taking the essential supremum over $V$ proves the embedding $\|\bm{B}\|_{\infty}\leq C_{b}\|\bm{B}\|_{H^{2}}$ . The series defining $C_{b}$ converges because its summand behaves as $\lambda_{mnk}^{-2}$ for large wavenumbers. ∎

## Appendix B Poloidal-Toroidal Decomposition

If magnetic flux is exact, a magnetic field $\bm{B}$ in the plane layer admits the poloidal-toroidal decomposition

$$ \bm{B}=\nabla\times\nabla\times\Phi\bm{e}_{z}+\nabla\times\Theta\bm{e}_{z}+\bm{B}^{0}=:\bm{B}^{\Phi}+\bm{B}^{\Theta}+\bm{B}^{0}. $$

Respectively, $\Phi$ and $\Theta$ are the scalar potentials for the poloidal and toroidal parts of the magnetic field $\bm{B}^{\Phi}$ and $\bm{B}^{\Theta}$ . In the plane layer, the representation is completed by the (horizontal) base field

$$ \bm{B}^{0}=B^{0}_{x}(z)\,\bm{e}_{x}+B^{0}_{y}(z)\,\bm{e}_{y}. $$

Clearly, for $\alpha\in\{\Phi,\Theta,0\}$ it holds

$$ \nabla\cdot\bm{B}^{\alpha}=0. $$

Here, we establish orthogonality in $L^{2}_{\mathrm{sol}}$ and provide representation formulae.

#### Proposition B.1.

If $\alpha\neq\beta\in\{\Phi,\Theta,0\}$ , then

$$ \langle\bm{B}^{\alpha},\bm{B}^{\beta}\rangle=0. $$

#### Proof.

Writing the volume integral as a vertical integral in $\mathrm{d}z$ of surface integrals in $\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y$ , it follows that

$$ \displaystyle\langle\bm{B}^{\Phi},\bm{B}^{\Theta}\rangle \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{d}z\int\bm{B}^{\Phi}\cdot\bm{B}^{\Theta}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{d}z\int\nabla_{x,y}\partial_{z}\Phi\cdot\nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\Theta\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y \displaystyle=-\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{d}z\int\partial_{z}\Phi\nabla_{x,y}\cdot\nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\Theta\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y=0. $$

In the last line, we integrated by parts on each surface using that $\nabla_{x,y}$ is tangent to the surface and that $\nabla_{x,y}\cdot\nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}=0$ in general.

For $\alpha\in\{\Phi,\Theta\}$ , it follows that

$$ \displaystyle\langle\bm{B}^{0},\bm{B}^{\alpha}\rangle \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{d}z\,\bm{B}^{0}\cdot\int\bm{B}^{\alpha}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y. \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{d}z\left(B^{0}_{x}\int B^{\alpha}_{x}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y+B^{0}_{y}\int B^{\alpha}_{y}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y\right)=0. $$

The last equality holds because in either case $\alpha=\Phi$ or $\alpha=\Theta$ , the components $B_{x}^{\alpha}$ and $B_{y}^{\alpha}$ are total derivatives in $\partial_{x}$ or $\partial_{y}$ . ∎

A basic observation is that the toroidal part is $\nabla_{x,y}$ -divergence free

$$ \nabla_{x,y}\cdot\bm{B}^{\Theta}=\partial_{x}B^{\Theta}_{x}+\partial_{y}B^{\Theta}_{y}=0, $$

and the poloidal part is $\nabla_{x,y}$ -curl free

$$ \nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\cdot\bm{B}^{\Phi}=\partial_{x}B^{\Phi}_{y}-\partial_{y}B^{\Phi}_{x}=0. $$

Clearly, the base part $\bm{B}^{0}$ is annihilated by $\nabla_{x,y}.$

#### Proposition B.2.

The scalar potential for the poloidal part has the representation

$$ \Phi(x,y,z)=\Phi(x,y,0)+\int_{0}^{z}\mathrm{d}z^{\prime}\,(\nabla_{x,y}^{2})^{-1}(\nabla_{x,y}\cdot\bm{B})(x,y,z^{\prime}). $$

#### Proof.

By divergence theorem,

$$ \int\nabla_{x,y}\cdot\bm{B}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y=0. $$

Thus $(-\nabla_{x,y}^{2})^{-1}$ is well defined on every constant $z$ surface. Then

$$ \nabla_{x,y}\cdot\bm{B}=\nabla_{x,y}\cdot\bm{B}^{\Phi}=\nabla_{x,y}^{2}\partial_{z}\Phi. $$

Inverting $\nabla_{x,y}^{2}$ and integrating in $\mathrm{d}z$ yields the claim. ∎

#### Proposition B.3.

The scalar potential for the toroidal part has the representation

$$ \Theta(x,y,z)=(\nabla_{x,y}^{2})^{-1}(\nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\cdot\bm{B})(x,y,z). $$

#### Proof.

Let us first verify that the $\nabla_{x,y}$ -curl has zero average on each constant $z$ surface. Indeed, after integrating by parts

$$ \int\nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\cdot\bm{B}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y=\int\mathrm{d}y\int\partial_{x}B_{y}\,\mathrm{d}x-\int\mathrm{d}x\int\partial_{y}B_{x}\,\mathrm{d}y=0 $$

and so $(-\nabla_{x,y}^{2})^{-1}$ in the representation is well defined. Pointwise it holds

$$ \nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\cdot\bm{B}^{\Phi}=\nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\cdot\nabla_{x,y}\partial_{z}\Phi=0. $$

Therefore, as claimed

$$ \nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\cdot\bm{B}=\nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\cdot\bm{B}^{\Theta}=\nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\cdot\nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\Theta=\nabla_{x,y}^{2}\Theta. $$

∎

On the other hand, the poloidal and toroidal part have zero horizontal mean, if $\alpha\in\{\Phi,\Theta\}$ then

$$ \bm{e}_{x}\int B_{x}^{\alpha}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y+\bm{e}_{y}\int B_{y}^{\alpha}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y=0. $$

Almost tautologically,

#### Proposition B.4.

The (horizontal) base part has the representation

$$ \bm{B}^{0}(z)=\bm{e}_{x}\int B_{x}(z)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y+\bm{e}_{y}\int B_{y}(z)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y. $$
